claim: In DC Comics, Superman's Kryptonian birth name is Kal-El.
explanation: Superman is born Kal-El on Krypton and raised on Earth as Clark Kent.

claim: In mainstream DC Comics, Alfred Pennyworth is Bruce Wayne's biological uncle.
explanation: Alfred is the Wayne family butler and Bruce's surrogate father figure, not a blood relative.

claim: In DC Comics, Wonder Woman's Lasso of Truth compels anyone bound by it to tell the truth.
explanation: The Lasso of Truth (Lasso of Hestia) forces those it binds to speak honestly.

claim: In DC Comics, Barry Allen's civilian job is as a photographer for the Daily Planet.
explanation: Barry Allen is a forensic scientist with the Central City Police Department. Photography at the Daily Planet is Jimmy Olsen's job.

claim: In modern DC Comics, Aquaman's parents are lighthouse keeper Tom Curry and Atlantean queen Atlanna.
explanation: Arthur Curry is the son of human lighthouse keeper Tom Curry and the Atlantean queen Atlanna.

claim: In DC Comics, Hal Jordan worked as a firefighter before becoming a Green Lantern.
explanation: Hal Jordan was a test pilot for Ferris Aircraft before receiving his power ring.

claim: In DC Comics, Cyborg's father, Silas Stone, is a scientist at S.T.A.R. Labs.
explanation: Silas Stone is a S.T.A.R. Labs scientist who saved his son Victor's life with cybernetic technology.

claim: In DC Comics, Martian Manhunter's primary weakness is kryptonite.
explanation: J'onn J'onzz's well-known weakness is fire. Kryptonite is associated with Kryptonians.

claim: In DC Comics, Green Arrow is the secret identity of billionaire Oliver Queen.
explanation: Oliver Queen is a wealthy industrialist who becomes the archer vigilante Green Arrow.

claim: In the 2019 film Shazam!, Zachary Levi plays the teenage Billy Batson.
explanation: Asher Angel plays teenage Billy Batson. Zachary Levi plays his adult superhero form, Shazam.

claim: In DC Comics, Supergirl (Kara Zor-El) is Superman's cousin.
explanation: Kara Zor-El is the daughter of Zor-El, brother of Superman's father Jor-El, making her Kal-El's cousin.

claim: In DC Comics, Supergirl (Kara Zor-El) was born on Earth.
explanation: Kara Zor-El was born on Krypton and sent to Earth as a teenager.

claim: In DC Comics, Dick Grayson was the first Robin, debuting in Detective Comics #38 (1940).
explanation: Dick Grayson debuted as Robin in Detective Comics #38 in April 1940.

claim: In DC Comics, Jason Todd was the first person to be Batman's sidekick Robin.
explanation: Dick Grayson was the first Robin. Jason Todd was the second.

claim: In DC Comics, Jaime Reyes, the third Blue Beetle, is from El Paso, Texas.
explanation: Jaime Reyes is a teenager from El Paso, Texas, who bonds with the Scarab.

claim: In DC Comics, the Scarab bonded to Jaime Reyes is a piece of ancient Atlantean technology.
explanation: The Scarab is alien technology created by the Reach, not Atlantean in origin.

claim: In DC Comics, Dick Grayson's Nightwing name was inspired by a Kryptonian vigilante in Superman stories.
explanation: Dick took the name from the legend of Nightwing, a Kryptonian hero that Superman told him about.

claim: In DC Comics, Nightwing's longtime base of operations is the city of Metropolis.
explanation: Nightwing is most closely associated with Blüdhaven and Gotham City, not Metropolis.

claim: In DC Comics, Hippolyta is the queen of the Amazons and Wonder Woman's mother.
explanation: Hippolyta rules the Amazons of Themyscira and is Diana's mother in the Wonder Woman mythos.

claim: In DC Comics, Superman's Fortress of Solitude is located in the Sahara Desert.
explanation: The Fortress of Solitude is traditionally located in the Arctic.

claim: In DC Comics, Clark Kent grew up in Smallville, Kansas, raised by Jonathan and Martha Kent.
explanation: Jonathan and Martha Kent raised Kal-El as Clark on their farm near Smallville, Kansas.

claim: In DC Comics, Lois Lane is a reporter for the Gotham Gazette.
explanation: Lois Lane works for the Daily Planet in Metropolis.

claim: In DC Comics, Batman first appeared in Detective Comics #27 in 1939.
explanation: Batman debuted in Detective Comics #27, cover-dated May 1939.

claim: In DC Comics, Superman first appeared in Action Comics #1 in 1945.
explanation: Superman debuted in Action Comics #1, cover-dated June 1938.

claim: In DC Comics, Barry Allen gained his speed powers when lightning struck chemicals in his lab.
explanation: A lightning bolt shattered a cabinet of chemicals that drenched Barry, granting him super-speed.

claim: In DC Comics, Wally West is the biological son of Barry Allen.
explanation: Wally West is Iris West Allen's nephew and Barry's protégé, not his son.

claim: In DC Comics, Green Lantern power rings are fueled by the emotional spectrum color of love.
explanation: Green Lantern rings are powered by willpower. Love belongs to the violet Star Sapphires.

claim: In DC Comics, the Green Lantern Corps was founded by the Guardians of the Universe and is headquartered on Oa.
explanation: The Guardians created the Corps, whose headquarters is the planet Oa.

claim: In DC Comics, Sinestro is from the planet Thanagar.
explanation: Sinestro is from the planet Korugar. Thanagar is Hawkman's homeworld.

claim: In DC Comics, Barry Allen died during Crisis on Infinite Earths (1985-86).
explanation: Barry Allen sacrificed himself in Crisis on Infinite Earths #8 to stop the Anti-Monitor's antimatter cannon.

claim: In DC Comics, Green Lantern John Stewart is an architect and former U.S. Marine.
explanation: John Stewart is portrayed as an architect who served in the U.S. Marine Corps.

claim: In DC Comics, Black Canary's signature power is the Canary Cry, a powerful sonic scream.
explanation: Dinah Lance's Canary Cry is her best-known metahuman ability.

claim: In DC Comics, Green Arrow's original sidekick Speedy is Wally West.
explanation: Speedy is Roy Harper. Wally West is Kid Flash, the Flash's sidekick.

claim: In DC Comics, Aquaman can communicate telepathically with marine life.
explanation: Telepathic communication with sea creatures is one of Aquaman's core abilities.

claim: In DC Comics, Aquaman's wife Mera was born in the kingdom of Atlantis.
explanation: Mera is from the dimension of Xebel, not Atlantis.

claim: In the DC Extended Universe, Henry Cavill plays Superman in Man of Steel (2013).
explanation: Henry Cavill starred as Clark Kent/Superman in Man of Steel.

claim: In the DC Extended Universe, Gal Gadot plays Wonder Woman in the 2017 film Wonder Woman.
explanation: Gal Gadot starred as Diana Prince/Wonder Woman in the 2017 film.

claim: In the CW's The Flash TV series, Grant Gustin plays Wally West.
explanation: Grant Gustin plays Barry Allen. Keiynan Lonsdale plays Wally West.

claim: In the 2023 film Blue Beetle, Xolo Maridueña plays Jaime Reyes.
explanation: Xolo Maridueña stars as Jaime Reyes in Blue Beetle.

claim: In the DC Extended Universe's Justice League (2017), Ezra Miller plays Cyborg.
explanation: Ray Fisher plays Cyborg. Ezra Miller plays Barry Allen/The Flash.

claim: In the TV series Supergirl, Melissa Benoist plays Kara Danvers.
explanation: Melissa Benoist stars as Kara Danvers/Supergirl in the series.

claim: In the TV series Supergirl, Kara Danvers works as a reporter at the Daily Planet.
explanation: In the series, Kara works at CatCo Worldwide Media in National City.

claim: In DC Comics, Ray Palmer, the Silver Age Atom, can shrink to subatomic size.
explanation: Ray Palmer uses white dwarf star matter to shrink himself, even to microscopic scales.

claim: In DC Comics, Zatanna casts her spells by speaking words backward.
explanation: Zatanna's magic is activated by reversed speech.

claim: In DC Comics, Hawkman's flight is enabled by a harness made of Nth metal.
explanation: Nth metal is an anti-gravity metal used in Hawkman's wings and harness.

claim: In DC Comics, Cyborg's father, Silas Stone, is an executive at LexCorp.
explanation: Silas Stone is a scientist at S.T.A.R. Labs, not a LexCorp executive.

claim: In DC Comics, the Green Lantern Corps is headquartered on the planet Daxam.
explanation: The Corps is headquartered on Oa. Daxam is a separate planet.

claim: In DC Comics, Wonder Woman's homeland, Themyscira, is hidden in the Himalayas.
explanation: Themyscira is an island hidden from the outside world, not a mountain realm.

claim: In DC Comics, Dick Grayson's parents were killed by Joe Chill.
explanation: Tony Zucco was responsible for the Graysons' deaths. Joe Chill murdered Bruce Wayne's parents.

claim: In DC Comics, Superman's biological father is named Zor-El.
explanation: Superman's father is Jor-El. Zor-El is Supergirl's father.

claim: In DC Comics, the Joker first appeared in Batman #1 (1940).
explanation: The Joker debuted in Batman #1, cover-dated Spring 1940.

claim: In Batman: The Killing Joke, the Joker shoots Commissioner Gordon, leaving him paralyzed.
explanation: The Joker shoots Barbara Gordon (Batgirl), paralyzing her, and then tortures Commissioner Gordon.

claim: In Batman: The Killing Joke, the Joker's suggested backstory is that of a failed comedian who wore a Red Hood.
explanation: The story presents an unreliable origin in which a struggling comedian takes part in a criminal heist as the Red Hood.

claim: In Superman comics, Lex Luthor is the billionaire head of LexCorp.
explanation: In the post-Crisis Superman comics, Lex Luthor is a wealthy industrialist who runs LexCorp.

claim: In Superman comics, LexCorp is headquartered in Gotham City.
explanation: LexCorp is based in Metropolis, Superman's home city.

claim: In the post-Crisis DC Universe, Lex Luthor was elected President of the United States.
explanation: Lex Luthor won the presidency in the post-Crisis DC Universe, a storyline that played out in the Superman and Batman titles.

claim: In DC Comics, Darkseid, ruler of Apokolips, relentlessly seeks the Anti-Life Equation.
explanation: The Anti-Life Equation, a formula for control over free will, is Darkseid's central goal.

claim: In DC Comics, Darkseid's son Orion was raised on Apokolips by Darkseid himself.
explanation: Orion was exchanged in a peace pact and raised on New Genesis by Highfather.

claim: In DC Comics, Reverse-Flash Eobard Thawne is a native of the 31st century.
explanation: Eobard Thawne comes from the 25th century.

claim: In the first season of the CW's The Flash, Eobard Thawne is revealed to have killed Barry Allen's mother, Nora.
explanation: The series establishes Thawne as the killer of Nora Allen.

claim: In DC Comics, General Zod first appeared in Adventure Comics #283 (1961).
explanation: Zod debuted in Adventure Comics #283 as a Kryptonian military officer.

claim: In Man of Steel (2013), General Zod is played by Terence Stamp.
explanation: Michael Shannon plays Zod in Man of Steel. Terence Stamp played him in Superman II (1980).

claim: In DC Comics, Brainiac shrank and bottled the Kryptonian city of Kandor.
explanation: Brainiac captured Kandor and kept it in a bottle, a long-standing part of Superman lore.

claim: In Silver Age DC Comics, Brainiac originates from the planet Daxam.
explanation: The Silver Age Brainiac, Vril Dox, is from the planet Colu. Daxam is a different planet.

claim: In DC Comics, Harley Quinn's real name is Harleen Quinzel, a former psychiatrist at Arkham Asylum.
explanation: Harleen Quinzel was Joker's psychiatrist at Arkham before becoming Harley Quinn.

claim: Harley Quinn first appeared in a DC comic book before debuting in animation.
explanation: Harley Quinn debuted in Batman: The Animated Series in 1992 and joined the comics afterward.

claim: In DC Comics, the first Cheetah was Priscilla Rich, who debuted in Wonder Woman #6 (1943).
explanation: Priscilla Rich was the original Cheetah, predating Barbara Minerva.

claim: In post-Crisis DC Comics, Barbara Minerva, the Cheetah, is a marine biologist.
explanation: Barbara Minerva is an archaeologist.

claim: In DC Comics, Deathstroke first appeared in The New Teen Titans #2 (1980).
explanation: Deathstroke was created by Marv Wolfman and George Perez and debuted in The New Teen Titans #2.

claim: In DC Comics, Slade Wilson served in the U.S. Navy before becoming Deathstroke.
explanation: Slade Wilson was a career U.S. Army soldier before his transformation.

claim: In the Knightfall storyline, Bane breaks Batman's back.
explanation: In Batman #497, Bane breaks Batman's back, putting Bruce Wayne out of action.

claim: In DC Comics, Bane was born in Gotham City's Blackgate Penitentiary.
explanation: Bane was born and raised in the Pena Duro prison on the island of Santa Prisca.

claim: In DC Comics, the Riddler first appeared in Detective Comics #140 (1948).
explanation: Edward Nygma debuted in Detective Comics #140.

claim: In Batman Forever (1995), Tommy Lee Jones plays the Riddler.
explanation: Jim Carrey plays the Riddler. Tommy Lee Jones plays Two-Face.

claim: In DC Comics, Scarecrow first appeared in World's Finest Comics #3 (1941).
explanation: Jonathan Crane debuted in World's Finest Comics #3.

claim: In DC Comics, Jonathan Crane, the Scarecrow, was a professor of chemistry.
explanation: Jonathan Crane was a psychology professor who specialized in fear.

claim: In Batman comics, Harvey Dent becomes Two-Face after mobster Sal Maroni throws acid on his face.
explanation: Maroni scars Dent's face with acid during a trial, splitting him into Two-Face.

claim: In Batman comics, Two-Face's coin is a standard coin with heads on one side and tails on the other.
explanation: The coin is double-headed, and one side is scarred.

claim: In DC Comics, Sinestro was once the mentor of Hal Jordan in the Green Lantern Corps.
explanation: Sinestro trained Hal Jordan before turning against the Guardians.

claim: In DC Comics, Black Adam draws his powers from the Greek gods.
explanation: Black Adam's powers come from Egyptian gods: Shu, Heru, Amon, Zehuti, Aton, and Mehen.

claim: In the film Black Adam (2022), Dwayne Johnson plays the title character.
explanation: Dwayne Johnson stars as Black Adam in the 2022 film.

claim: In DC Comics, Doomsday killed Superman in Superman #75 (1993).
explanation: The Death of Superman storyline concluded in Superman #75.

claim: In DC Comics, Doomsday was originally created on Apokolips.
explanation: Doomsday was created through genetic experiments on prehistoric Krypton.

claim: In DC Comics, Ra's al Ghul's daughter is Talia al Ghul.
explanation: Talia al Ghul is Ra's al Ghul's daughter and the mother of Damian Wayne.

claim: In DC Comics, Ra's al Ghul leads the Court of Owls.
explanation: Ra's al Ghul leads the League of Assassins. The Court of Owls is a separate secret society in Gotham.

claim: In DC Comics, Black Manta first appeared in Aquaman #35 (1967).
explanation: Black Manta debuted in Aquaman #35.

claim: In DC Comics, Ocean Master (Orm) is Aquaman's cousin.
explanation: Orm is Aquaman's half-brother.

claim: In DC Comics, the Penguin, Oswald Cobblepot, runs a Gotham club called the Iceberg Lounge.
explanation: The Iceberg Lounge is the Penguin's nightclub and criminal front.

claim: In DC Comics, Poison Ivy, Pamela Isley, was a trained zoologist.
explanation: Pamela Isley was a botanist.

claim: In Batman: The Animated Series, Mister Freeze's tragic origin as a scientist saving his wife Nora debuts in the episode Heart of Ice.
explanation: Heart of Ice reimagined Victor Fries as a sympathetic cryogenicist trying to save Nora.

claim: In DC Comics, Captain Cold's cold gun was built by Mister Freeze.
explanation: Leonard Snart built his own cold gun.

claim: In DC Comics, Gorilla Grodd comes from the hidden Gorilla City in Africa.
explanation: Grodd is a super-intelligent telepathic gorilla from Gorilla City, hidden in Africa.

claim: In DC Comics, Superman villain Metallo is John Corben, whose power source is a kryptonite heart.
explanation: John Corben is a cyborg whose kryptonite heart weakens Superman.

claim: In DC Comics, Mister Mxyzptlk can be sent home by tricking him into saying his name backward.
explanation: Saying his name backward sends the imp back to the Fifth Dimension.

claim: Joaquin Phoenix won the Academy Award for Best Supporting Actor for Joker (2019).
explanation: Phoenix won the Academy Award for Best Actor for Joker.

claim: In The Dark Knight Rises (2012), Anne Hathaway plays Poison Ivy.
explanation: Anne Hathaway plays Selina Kyle, who is referred to as Catwoman in the film's credits.

claim: In Man of Steel (2013), Jesse Eisenberg plays Lex Luthor.
explanation: Eisenberg first played Lex Luthor in Batman v Superman: Dawn of Justice (2016). Lex is not a character in Man of Steel.
source_name: Wikipedia: Batman v Superman: Dawn of Justice

claim: In Superman (1978), Lex Luthor is played by Kevin Spacey.
explanation: Gene Hackman plays Lex Luthor in Superman (1978). Kevin Spacey played him in Superman Returns (2006).

claim: In Tim Burton's Batman (1989), the Joker is played by Cesar Romero.
explanation: Jack Nicholson plays the Joker in the 1989 film. Cesar Romero played him in the 1960s TV series.

claim: In DC Comics, the first Clayface, Basil Karlo, was a chemist before his transformation.
explanation: Basil Karlo was a horror-film actor who took on the Clayface identity.

claim: In DC Comics, the Green Lantern Corps is headquartered on the planet Oa, home of the Guardians of the Universe.
explanation: Oa, at the center of the universe, houses the Central Power Battery and the Guardians, who founded the Corps.

claim: In DC Comics, the Guardians of the Universe are based on the sentient planet Mogo.
explanation: The Guardians are based on Oa. Mogo is a separate sentient planet that serves as a Green Lantern.

claim: In DC Comics, Kyle Rayner received his Green Lantern ring from Ganthet, the last surviving Guardian after Hal Jordan's fall.
explanation: After Hal Jordan destroyed the Central Power Battery and most Guardians were lost, Ganthet gave Kyle the last power ring.

claim: In DC Comics, standard Green Lantern rings are powered by the emotion of fear.
explanation: Green Lantern rings are powered by willpower (green). Fear is the yellow light, used by Sinestro Corps rings.

claim: In classic Green Lantern comics, a power ring was famously ineffective against anything yellow.
explanation: The 'yellow impurity' was the ring's classic weakness in Silver Age comics, and later continuity tied it to the yellow light of fear.

claim: In DC Comics, Alan Scott received his Green Lantern ring from the dying alien Abin Sur.
explanation: Abin Sur passed his ring to Hal Jordan. Alan Scott's power came from a magical green lantern and the Starheart/Green Flame.

claim: In DC Comics, Mogo is a sentient planet that serves as a member of the Green Lantern Corps.
explanation: Mogo, 'the Planet That Walks Like a Man', is a living world and a Green Lantern.

claim: In DC Comics, the Sinestro Corps was first formed during the Blackest Night storyline (2009).
explanation: The Sinestro Corps debuted in the 2007 Sinestro Corps War storyline. Blackest Night (2009-2010) introduced the Black Lanterns and a full emotional spectrum of Corps.

claim: In the DC Comics event Blackest Night, the Black Lantern rings are powered by death.
explanation: The Black Lantern Corps, led by Nekron, uses the black light of death to reanimate the dead.

claim: In DC Comics, Raven of the Teen Titans is the daughter of the demon lord Trigon.
explanation: Raven's mother Arella was bound to Trigon, making Raven his half-human, half-demon daughter.

claim: In DC Comics, Starfire (Koriand'r) comes from the planet Thanagar.
explanation: Starfire is from the planet Tamaran. Thanagar is the home of Hawkman and Hawkgirl.

claim: In DC Comics, the original Teen Titans debuted in The Brave and the Bold #54 (1964) with Robin, Kid Flash, and Aqualad.
explanation: The Brave and the Bold #54 featured the three sidekicks teaming up, and the group was later named the Teen Titans.

claim: In DC Comics, Cyborg (Victor Stone) was a founding member of the original 1960s Teen Titans.
explanation: Cyborg was created in 1980 for The New Teen Titans by Marv Wolfman and George Perez, not the 1960s team.

claim: In DC Comics, Amanda Waller leads the government black-ops program Task Force X, also known as the Suicide Squad.
explanation: Since John Ostrander's 1987 series, Waller has been the Squad's director, using imprisoned villains for covert missions.

claim: In DC Comics, Suicide Squad member Captain Boomerang (George 'Digger' Harkness) is from New Zealand.
explanation: Digger Harkness is Australian, and he is a longtime enemy of the Flash.

claim: Harley Quinn first appeared in Batman: The Animated Series (1992) before being added to DC's comic book continuity.
explanation: Harley debuted in the 1992 episode 'Joker's Favor' and joined the comics later.

claim: In DC Comics, the Legion of Super-Heroes first appeared in Adventure Comics #247 (1958).
explanation: The team debuted in a Superboy story, set in the future, in Adventure Comics #247.

claim: In classic Legion of Super-Heroes comics, Brainiac 5 was one of the three founding members.
explanation: The founders were Cosmic Boy, Saturn Girl, and Lightning Lad. Brainiac 5 joined later.

claim: In post-Crisis DC Comics, Barbara Gordon became the information broker Oracle after being shot and paralyzed by the Joker in The Killing Joke.
explanation: After her injury in Batman: The Killing Joke (1988), Barbara reinvented herself as Oracle and later co-led the Birds of Prey.

claim: In DC Comics, Helena Bertinelli, the Huntress of the Birds of Prey, is the biological daughter of Bruce Wayne.
explanation: Helena Bertinelli is the daughter of Mafia boss Franco Bertinelli. The Earth-2 Huntress, Helena Wayne, is Bruce Wayne's daughter.

claim: In mainstream DC Comics, Tim Drake was the second person to be Robin.
explanation: Dick Grayson was the first Robin, Jason Todd was the second, and Tim Drake was the third.

claim: In mainstream DC Comics, Damian Wayne is the biological son of Bruce Wayne and Talia al Ghul.
explanation: Damian was raised by the League of Assassins before joining his father as Robin.

claim: In DC Comics, Stephanie Brown, known as Spoiler, briefly served as Robin in the mid-2000s.
explanation: Stephanie took up the Robin identity for a short time around 2004, as Tim Drake stepped back from the role.

claim: In DC Comics, Cassandra Cain was the first character to be Batgirl, before Barbara Gordon.
explanation: Barbara Gordon debuted as Batgirl in 1967. Cassandra Cain took the name in the late 1990s.

claim: In the Knightfall storyline, Dick Grayson replaced a broken Bruce Wayne as Batman.
explanation: After Bane broke Bruce's back, Jean-Paul Valley (Azrael) became Batman. Dick Grayson took the cowl in later years.

claim: In DC Comics, the Court of Owls debuted in Batman vol. 2 #1 (2011) by Scott Snyder and Greg Capullo.
explanation: The secret society, which uses assassins called Talons, was introduced in the New 52 relaunch of Batman.

claim: In DC Comics, Superman's home planet Krypton orbited a yellow sun.
explanation: Krypton orbited the red sun Rao. Earth's yellow sun gives Kryptonians their powers.

claim: In DC Comics, Supergirl (Kara Zor-El) is Superman's younger sister.
explanation: Kara Zor-El is Superman's cousin, the daughter of Jor-El's brother Zor-El.

claim: In Pre-Crisis Superman comics, Gold Kryptonite permanently removes a Kryptonian's powers.
explanation: Gold Kryptonite is one of the few varieties capable of permanently stripping Kryptonians of their powers.

claim: In DC Comics, a Mother Box can open Boom Tubes, the teleportation tunnels used by the New Gods.
explanation: Mother Boxes are sentient New Gods devices created by Jack Kirby, and they can create Boom Tubes.

claim: In DC Comics, Boom Tubes are teleportation tunnels powered by the Speed Force.
explanation: Boom Tubes are New Gods technology tied to Mother Boxes, not the Speed Force.

claim: In DC Comics, the Speed Force is an extradimensional energy source that grants speedsters like the Flash their powers.
explanation: The Speed Force is the source of speedsters' abilities, including those of Barry Allen and Wally West.

claim: In DC Comics, Barry Allen was the first character to use the name the Flash.
explanation: Jay Garrick was the first Flash, debuting in Flash Comics #1 in 1940. Barry Allen came in 1956.

claim: In Crisis on Infinite Earths #8, Barry Allen died while destroying the Anti-Monitor's antimatter cannon.
explanation: Barry's sacrifice stopped the cannon and became the Pre-Crisis Flash's defining death.

claim: In post-Crisis DC Comics, Wally West is Barry Allen's biological brother.
explanation: Wally is Iris West's nephew and became Barry's sidekick Kid Flash. He is not Barry's brother.

claim: In DC Comics, the Reverse-Flash Eobard Thawne is a native of the 25th century.
explanation: Thawne comes from the 25th century and became obsessed with Barry Allen after learning of his legacy.

claim: In post-Crisis DC Comics, Wonder Woman was sculpted from clay by Hippolyta and given life by the gods.
explanation: George Perez's 1987 relaunch made Diana a child born of clay on Themyscira, not of a human father.

claim: In post-Crisis DC Comics, Wonder Woman's Lasso of Truth was forged by the war god Ares.
explanation: In the post-Crisis version, the lasso was forged by Hephaestus from Gaea's girdle. Ares is Diana's enemy.

claim: In modern DC Comics, Aquaman (Arthur Curry) is the son of the lighthouse keeper Tom Curry and the Atlantean queen Atlanna.
explanation: Arthur is half-human and half-Atlantean and was raised by his father before becoming king of Atlantis.

claim: In DC Comics, Aquaman's wife Mera is a native of Atlantis.
explanation: Mera comes from the dimension of Xebel, not Atlantis.

claim: The Justice Society of America debuted in All Star Comics #3 (1940) and is considered the first superhero team in comics.
explanation: All Star Comics #3 brought together DC's Golden Age heroes, making the JSA the first superhero team.

claim: In the Silver Age Justice League of America (1960), Green Arrow was a founding member.
explanation: The founders were Flash, Green Lantern, Aquaman, Martian Manhunter, and Wonder Woman. Green Arrow joined later.

claim: In DC Comics, Orion is Darkseid's son but was raised on New Genesis by Highfather.
explanation: Orion was exchanged as a child in a peace pact between Apokolips and New Genesis.

claim: In DC Comics, Mister Miracle (Scott Free) is the biological son of Darkseid.
explanation: Scott Free is Highfather's son, raised on Apokolips in the exchange with Orion.

claim: In DC Comics, Darkseid of Apokolips seeks the Anti-Life Equation.
explanation: The equation would allow Darkseid to control all sentient life.

claim: In DC Comics, Darkseid is the ruler of New Genesis.
explanation: Darkseid rules Apokolips. New Genesis is led by Highfather.

claim: In DC Comics, the Dark Multiverse was introduced in the 2017 Dark Nights: Metal event.
explanation: The concept of the Dark Multiverse, a realm of nightmarish alternate realities, was introduced in the Metal event.

claim: In Pre-Crisis DC Comics, the Justice League of America lived on Earth-2.
explanation: The Justice League lived on Earth-One. Earth-2 was home to the Golden Age Justice Society.

claim: In DC Comics, the 1994 event Zero Hour: Crisis in Time led directly to the New 52 relaunch.
explanation: The New 52 followed Flashpoint (2011). Zero Hour (1994) was a separate continuity-tightening event.

claim: In DC Comics, Owlman of the Crime Syndicate of America is the Earth-3 counterpart of Superman.
explanation: Owlman is Earth-3's Batman counterpart. Ultraman is the Superman counterpart.

claim: In DC Comics, the magic word SHAZAM stands for six figures: Solomon, Hercules, Atlas, Zeus, Achilles, and Mercury.
explanation: Each letter names a figure whose attribute (wisdom, strength, stamina, power, courage, speed) Billy Batson gains when he speaks the word.

claim: In DC Comics, Billy Batson receives his powers from a wizard named Merlin.
explanation: The wizard who empowers Billy is named Shazam, not Merlin.

claim: Captain Marvel, now known as Shazam, first appeared in Fawcett Comics' Whiz Comics #2 (1940).
explanation: Captain Marvel debuted in Whiz Comics #2, cover-dated February 1940, from Fawcett Comics, not DC.

claim: In DC Comics, Black Adam is Billy Batson's long-lost older brother.
explanation: Black Adam is Teth-Adam, an ancient Egyptian champion who was once empowered by the wizard Shazam. He is not related to Billy.

claim: DC's 1970s series featuring Captain Marvel was titled Shazam! because Marvel Comics held the trademark on the name Captain Marvel for comic books.
explanation: DC licensed the Fawcett characters but couldn't use the Captain Marvel title on its cover, so the series launched in 1973 as Shazam!.

claim: In DC Comics, Dr. Thaddeus Sivana is Superman's greatest archenemy.
explanation: Dr. Sivana is the archenemy of Captain Marvel (Shazam). Superman's greatest archenemy is Lex Luthor.

claim: In Fawcett's original Golden Age comics, Mary Marvel is Billy Batson's twin sister, Mary Batson.
explanation: Mary Batson was introduced in 1942 as Billy's long-lost twin who gains similar powers by saying SHAZAM.

claim: In the original Fawcett Captain Marvel comics, the villain Mister Mind is a worm from the planet Mars.
explanation: In the original comics, Mister Mind is an alien worm from Venus, not Mars.

claim: Black Adam first appeared in The Marvel Family #1 (1945), published by Fawcett Comics.
explanation: Black Adam debuted in The Marvel Family #1 (December 1945) as a Fawcett villain, long before DC's acquisition of the character.

claim: In DC Comics, Alfred Pennyworth debuted in Batman #16 (1943).
explanation: Alfred first appeared in Batman #16 in 1943.

claim: In mainstream DC Comics, the Joker is the man who murdered Thomas and Martha Wayne.
explanation: In mainstream comics, the killer is Joe Chill. Making Jack Napier the killer is a feature of the 1989 Batman film.

claim: In DC Comics, James Gordon appeared in Batman's first story, Detective Comics #27 (1939).
explanation: Gordon appeared in Detective Comics #27 as a police commissioner, in the first Batman story.

claim: In DC Comics, Bane was born and raised in Gotham City.
explanation: Bane was born in a prison on the Caribbean island of Santa Prisca.

claim: In DC Comics, Bat-Mite is an imp from the fifth dimension who admires Batman.
explanation: Bat-Mite, who debuted in Detective Comics #267 (1959), is a fifth-dimensional imp.

claim: In DC Comics, Harvey Dent was the district attorney of Metropolis before becoming Two-Face.
explanation: Harvey Dent was Gotham City's district attorney.

claim: In the classic DC Comics origin of Two-Face, the acid that scarred Harvey Dent was thrown by the mobster Sal Maroni.
explanation: In the comics, Sal Maroni threw acid in Dent's face during a trial.

claim: In DC Comics, Jonathan Crane, the Scarecrow, is a chemistry professor.
explanation: Crane is a professor of psychology who experiments with fear.

claim: In DC Comics, Poison Ivy's real name is Harleen Quinzel.
explanation: Poison Ivy is Pamela Isley. Harleen Quinzel is Harley Quinn.

claim: Mr. Freeze's tragic backstory about his wife Nora originated in Batman: The Animated Series (1992) and was later adopted into DC Comics.
explanation: The episode 'Heart of Ice' reimagined Mr. Freeze as a sympathetic villain, and the comics later adopted that origin.

claim: Detective Renee Montoya first appeared in Batman: The Animated Series before being added to DC Comics.
explanation: Montoya was created for the 1992 animated series and was later introduced into the comics.

claim: Jimmy Olsen first appeared in the Adventures of Superman radio show in 1940 before appearing in comics.
explanation: The radio show introduced Jimmy Olsen in 1940, and he later appeared in the Superman comics.

claim: In his first comic appearance, Action Comics #23 (1940), Lex Luthor was bald.
explanation: Luthor was drawn with red hair in his first appearance. His signature baldness came later.

claim: In Pre-Crisis comics, Bizarro debuted in Superboy #68 (1958) as an imperfect duplicate created by a duplicating ray.
explanation: The first Bizarro was an imperfect copy of Superboy made with a duplicator ray.

claim: Lois Lane first appeared in Action Comics #20 (1939).
explanation: Lois Lane debuted in Action Comics #1 (1938), alongside Superman.

claim: In his earliest 1938 comic stories, Superman could leap great distances but could not fly.
explanation: Early Superman stories showed him leaping, and flight came later.

claim: In DC Comics, Jor-El, Superman's biological father, was a Kryptonian military general.
explanation: Jor-El was a Kryptonian scientist who predicted the planet's destruction. General Zod was a military leader.

claim: In Pre-Crisis Superman comics, Brainiac is a native of Krypton.
explanation: Pre-Crisis, Brainiac is Vril Dox, a native of the planet Colu.

claim: Wonder Woman first appeared in All Star Comics #8 (1941).
explanation: Her first appearance was in All Star Comics #8, and her own title followed.

claim: Wonder Woman was created by Batman co-creator Bob Kane.
explanation: Wonder Woman was created by psychologist William Moulton Marston, with artist H. G. Peter.

claim: In Golden Age Wonder Woman comics, Etta Candy first appeared in Sensation Comics #2 (1942).
explanation: Etta Candy, Diana's friend, debuted in Sensation Comics #2.

claim: In DC Comics, Wally West debuted in The Flash #110 (1959).
explanation: Wally West was introduced in The Flash #110 as Kid Flash, Barry Allen's sidekick.

claim: In DC Comics, the Flash villain Captain Cold uses a heat gun.
explanation: Captain Cold (Leonard Snart) uses a cold gun.

claim: In DC Comics, John Stewart debuted in Green Lantern #87 (1971), created by Denny O'Neil and Neal Adams.
explanation: John Stewart debuted in Green Lantern vol. 2 #87 and was the first Black Green Lantern.

claim: In DC Comics, Guy Gardner is Hal Jordan's younger brother.
explanation: Guy Gardner is not related to Hal Jordan. Hal's brothers are Jack and Jim Jordan.

claim: In DC Comics, Kyle Rayner worked as a test pilot before becoming a Green Lantern.
explanation: Kyle Rayner was a struggling freelance artist. Hal Jordan was the test pilot.

claim: In DC Comics, Dick Grayson's Nightwing name was inspired by a Kryptonian legend that Superman related to him.
explanation: The name Nightwing comes from a Kryptonian legend of a hero called Nightwing that Superman told Dick Grayson.

claim: In DC Comics, Dick Grayson's parents were killed by the Joker.
explanation: Dick's parents, the Flying Graysons, were killed by the mobster Tony Zucco.

claim: In the DC Comics storyline A Death in the Family, Jason Todd was killed by the Penguin.
explanation: The Joker beat Jason Todd and then left him to die in an explosion.

claim: In DC Comics, Robin debuted in Detective Comics #27 (1939), alongside Batman's first appearance.
explanation: Robin debuted in Detective Comics #38 (1940). Batman's own debut was in Detective Comics #27.

claim: In DC Comics, Supergirl (Kara Zor-El) first appeared in Action Comics #252 (1959).
explanation: Kara debuted in Action Comics #252 in July 1959.

claim: In Pre-Crisis DC Comics, Supergirl's pet Streaky is a Kryptonian dog.
explanation: Streaky is a cat, the Super-Cat.

claim: In Pre-Crisis DC Comics, Krypto the Superdog first appeared in Adventure Comics #210 (1955).
explanation: Krypto was introduced in 1955 as Superboy's dog.

claim: The 1996 DC miniseries Kingdom Come was written by Mark Waid and painted by Alex Ross.
explanation: Mark Waid wrote Kingdom Come and Alex Ross painted it.

claim: The Elseworlds comic Superman: Red Son was written by Grant Morrison.
explanation: Mark Millar wrote Superman: Red Son.

claim: In DC Comics, Ted Kord, the second Blue Beetle, has no superpowers and relies on gadgets and intellect.
explanation: Ted Kord is a non-powered inventor and fighter.

claim: In DC Comics, Booster Gold is a former football player from the 25th century.
explanation: Booster Gold, who debuted in 1986, is a time traveler from the 25th century.

claim: In DC Comics, Plastic Man was a criminal named Eel O'Brian before gaining his powers.
explanation: Eel O'Brian was a crook who was doused in acid and gained stretching powers.

claim: In DC Comics, Oliver Queen, Green Arrow, is based in Metropolis.
explanation: Green Arrow is based in Star City (originally Seattle).

claim: In DC Comics, Gorilla City is hidden in South America.
explanation: Gorilla City is hidden in Africa.

claim: In DC Comics, Martian Manhunter's primary weakness is cold.
explanation: Martian Manhunter's primary weakness is fire.
